title: How do banks make money, and what matters in a banking case?
description: Retail banking economics for case interviews: net interest margin, fees, cost-to-income ratio, branches versus digital, and credit risk, with a worked…
hook: Banking cases can feel intimidating if you have never worked in finance, but the core economics are simple. A bank borrows money cheaply, lends it at a higher rate, charges fees and tries to keep costs and bad loans under control.
body:
How banks make money

  • Net interest income: the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits.
  • Fees: accounts, cards, payments, advice.

A worked example: net interest margin

A bank lends £10B at an average 6% and pays 3% on £10B of deposits. Net interest income: £600M − £300M = £300M. If rates fall and loan rates drop to 5% while deposit rates stay near 3%, income falls to £200M, a third less.

The cost side

The cost-to-income ratio (operating costs divided by income) shows efficiency. Branches, IT and staff are the big lines. Many banks are shifting customers to apps to cut branch and call-centre costs (see the cost reduction guide).

Credit risk

Loans that are not repaid become losses. Growing lending quickly by lowering standards can lift revenue now and losses later.

Typical banking case questions

  • Why have mortgage applications fallen?
  • How can we cut operating costs by 15%?
  • Should we launch a digital-only bank?
  • Why are our app ratings worse than rivals'?

Keep interest spread, credit losses and capital separate

Imagine a simple lender with £1 billion of average loans earning 7% interest, funded by £900 million of deposits paying 3% and £100 million of equity. Annual interest income is £70 million and deposit interest expense is £27 million. Its simplified net interest income is £43 million. That does not mean £43 million of profit: loan defaults, staff, technology, branches, regulation and tax still matter.

If expected credit losses equal 1.5% of the loan book, subtract another £15 million, leaving £28 million before operating costs. If those costs are £20 million, illustrative pre-tax profit is £8 million. Increasing loan volume sounds attractive, but it may require more deposits, more equity and greater exposure to borrowers who cannot repay. Ask whether growth improves risk-adjusted returns, rather than assuming every new loan is good business.

In a deposit-pricing case, split the question into customer retention, funding costs and alternatives. Raising the deposit rate by 0.5 percentage points on £900 million raises annual expense by £4.5 million, unless balances or account mix change. Could the bank attract enough extra deposits to replace more expensive wholesale funding? The answer depends on what those new balances are worth.

A good case recommendation states the relevant profitability metric, tests downside credit scenarios and notes regulatory capital constraints. Always distinguish interest income, net interest income and net profit.
